title: August 1 deadline hits: US frontier-model framework due today under EO 14409
subtitle: Treasury, NSA and CISA are required to publish a classified benchmarking process and a voluntary pre-release framework for covered frontier models today — 60 days after Trump signed the June 2 executive order.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Today is the 60-day deadline set by Executive Order 14409, which President Trump signed on June 2. Two deliverables are due. First, the National Security Agency — in consultation with CISA, the National Cyber Director, and the Department of War — must publish a classified benchmarking process for assessing the advanced cyber capabilities of AI models and determining when one qualifies as a 'covered frontier model.' Second, Treasury, NSA and CISA together must finalize a voluntary framework through which AI developers can engage the federal government before releasing a covered frontier model to trusted partners, including up to 30 days of pre-release federal access.

The mechanism worth understanding is that this is voluntary and it is opt-in. The order expressly disclaims any mandatory licensing regime, any preclearance requirement, and any permit for AI development. What it creates instead is a lane: a lab that wants to demonstrate good faith with the federal government can submit a model for 30-day review before release, and in exchange gets a private channel for feedback on cyber risk. A lab that does not want to submit is not required to. In practice, OpenAI and Anthropic have both signaled they will participate. Meta has not, and is notably absent from the deal.

In the last-six-months context, this is the second major AI regulatory event this week — the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency rules begin enforcement tomorrow, August 2. The two frameworks are structurally opposite. The EU is prescriptive and mandatory, with chatbot disclosure, deepfake labelling, and machine-readable marking of AI-generated content applying to any provider serving the EU market. The US framework is voluntary, opt-in, and focused narrowly on cybersecurity risk to national security. A developer serving both markets now has to think about compliance in two very different registers at once — one that treats AI as a consumer-protection issue, and one that treats it as a defense issue.

For learners: if you are studying AI policy, this week is the cleanest side-by-side comparison you will get of the two dominant regulatory philosophies. Read the EO 14409 text and Article 50 of the EU AI Act back to back — the divergence in what each considers the primary risk (national-security cyber threats vs. consumer deception) tells you more about how the West thinks about AI than any think-tank white paper. If you are building a product, the practical answer is that the EU rules will shape your UX starting tomorrow; the US framework will shape your government-relations strategy over the coming year.
